paper.cite: Sorsa, A., Tretow, A., Xu, W., Gerike, G., Lohvansuu, K., Hamalainen, J. A., & Leppanen, P. H. T. (2026). International Journal of Psychophysiology, 222, 113339.
paper.sample: Jyvaskyla Longitudinal Study of Dyslexia (JLD), adults 26-28 y, followed from birth

questions.text: Do the ERP group differences to these speech sounds seen at 9.5 y persist into adulthood?
In adulthood, do combined M/EEG source responses correlate with reading and reading-related skills?

design.text: Three groups by CHILDHOOD reading status, not adult status: RDFR (childhood reading difficulty + family risk, N=17), TRFR (typical reader + family risk, N=37), TRC (typical reader, no risk, N=37). RQ1 used EEG from N=91; RQ2 used combined M/EEG from N=84 (7 dropped for MEG quality).
design.why_it_matters: The grouping is retrospective, chosen to match Lohvansuu et al. (2014) so childhood and adulthood are comparable. RQ1 and RQ2 therefore run on different samples.

design.text: Passive oddball while watching a silent movie. Standard /at:a/ 80% (1000 trials); deviants /ata/ 10% (125, phonemic length) and /ap:a/ 10% (125, place of articulation). 25 min.
design.why_it_matters: Two deviants probe two different phonetic features. The whole result hinges on which of the two shows a group difference.

design.text: /at:a/ and /ap:a/ 450 ms, /ata/ 300 ms; deviant feature sits in the MIDDLE of the pseudoword. Only the silent gap differs between /ata/ (95 ms) and /at:a/ (255 ms). 34 ms constant onset delay from the stimulation system.
design.why_it_matters: Mid-word deviants and the length difference are why difference waves could not be computed (see L4) and why comparison with other adult studies is indirect (see L3).

design.text: RQ1: threshold-free cluster enhancement + permutation (5000), 50-900 ms, alpha .05, 9 comparisons (3 group pairs x 3 stimuli). RQ2: cluster-based permutation correlations, 12 tests (3 stimuli x 4 measures).
design.why_it_matters: No multiple-comparison correction across the 9 or the 12; the authors flag this for the 9 (see L2).

results.text: In adulthood RDFR still scored lower than both other groups on reading fluency (F(2,88)=24.87, p<.001, eta2=0.36), reading accuracy (F(2,88)=9.67, p<.001, eta2=0.18) and rapid naming (F(2,86)=7.70, p<.001, eta2=0.15). No TRFR-TRC differences.

Repeated-measures ANOVA childhood vs adulthood: fluency showed no time effect (F(1,79)=1.45, p=.233) but a group effect (F(2,79)=29.56, p<.001, eta2p=0.43); accuracy improved with time (F(1,79)=5.57, p=.021) with a group effect (F(2,79)=16.69, p<.001, eta2p=0.30). No time x group interaction for either (p=.743; p=.236).

Grand-average waveform (N=91) at Fz, onset-delay corrected: N1 93 ms, P2 151 ms; for /ata/ MMN 281 ms, P3a 351 ms, late negativity (LDN or RON) 483 ms; for /ap:a/ one long change-detection response 437-593 ms with no MMN/LDN separation.
results.why_it_matters: Establishes that the paradigm elicited the expected components before any group comparison.

results.where: Sec 3.1.2, Fig. 5 panels A & C p.9
results.text: For deviant /ap:a/ only: RDFR showed STRONGER responses than TRFR across midline, left and right channels, from 152 ms to 800 ms (TFCE cluster permutation, corrected p<.05).
results.direction_note: Enhanced, not attenuated -- the opposite of the modal finding in the wider dyslexia literature.

results.where: Sec 3.1.2, Fig. 5 panels B & D p.9
results.text: RDFR also showed stronger responses than TRC for /ap:a/, at left-hemisphere channels, around the 300 ms and 600 ms windows.
No significant TRC vs TRFR difference for /ap:a/.
results.why_it_matters: Family risk alone did not produce the effect; childhood reading difficulty did.

results.text: No significant group differences for the length deviant /ata/ or for the standard /at:a/ -- although at 9.5 y in the largely overlapping sample it was /ata/ that separated the groups (Lohvansuu et al., 2014).
results.direction_note: This is the paper's central developmental claim, and it rests on a null.

results.text: Source activity was predominantly in left and right auditory cortices for all speech sounds.
results.why_it_matters: Confirms the source model is picking up auditory responses, which is the precondition for the RQ2 correlations to be meaningful.

results.text: No significant correlations between source-level M/EEG activity and reading fluency, reading accuracy, RAN or working memory. Across all 12 combinations the correlation distributions were near-normal and centred near zero (mean r -0.05 to +0.09; SD 0.086-0.106); the share exceeding the uncorrected |r|>0.215 ran 1.4%-11.8% against a 5% chance expectation.
results.direction_note: The strongest form of the RQ2 answer, and also a null. The histogram check is what makes it more than an underpowered non-finding.

author_interpretations.text: The feature that separates the groups shifts across development (length at 9.5 y, place of articulation in adulthood), attributed to maturation plus continued exposure to speech making different linguistic features salient at different ages.
author_interpretations.boundary: A cross-age comparison of two significant-vs-null patterns, not a tested interaction. The authors do not test the age x feature interaction directly.

author_interpretations.text: Behavioural group differences were stable rather than widening, which the authors say contrasts with the Matthew effect (Stanovich, 1986).
author_interpretations.boundary: Rests on a non-significant time x group interaction -- absence of widening, not evidence of equivalence. The authors also note participants received varying intervention support over the follow-up.

author_interpretations.text: Enhanced responses in the JLD dyslexia group are read as compensation: more neurons recruited, working harder to encode the stimulus. At 6.5 y the same enhancement was instead attributed to larger, less specific neuronal populations (maturational).
author_interpretations.boundary: Two different mechanistic stories have been attached to the same directional finding at different ages. Neither is tested here.

author_interpretations.text: The authors name an unresolved conflict: elsewhere, enhanced responses to native speech deviancy are taken to reflect BETTER speech processing and reading, which is the opposite of what enhancement means in the JLD dyslexia group.
author_interpretations.boundary: Explicitly left unresolved by the authors. This is the sharpest open question in the paper.

author_interpretations.text: The childhood brain-behaviour link is gone in adulthood because adult reading is shaped by many other factors (exposure, strategies), and because speech processing itself keeps changing with exposure; the two may develop apart.
author_interpretations.boundary: A post-hoc explanation of a null. No mediator or moderator was tested.

limitations_author_acknowledged.text: The experimental setup changed across measurement points: at 6 months and 6.5 y short /ata/ was the standard with long /at:a/ as deviants; from 9.5 y onward long /at:a/ was the standard.

Nine group comparisons were run, which inflates Type I error. The authors state that choosing a correction is not straightforward given longitudinal priors and non-independent effects -- and apply none.

The deviant feature sits mid-pseudoword, unlike most adult studies which put the place-of-articulation contrast at onset; this may cause masking or extra processing demand and may explain divergence from other samples.

Difference waves could not be computed, because obligatory responses track the physical timing of syllables and the stimuli differ in length. The authors argue the standard showed no group difference, so the deviant effect is likely stimulus-specific.
Sample sizes differ across measurement points through attrition and splitting; 9.5 y and adulthood overlap substantially (79 measured with EEG at both ages).

limitations_analyst_raised.text: The dyslexia group is N=17 against N=37 and N=37. The paper's two headline developmental claims (R7, no /ata/ difference; R9, no brain-behaviour correlation) are both nulls resting on that cell. No power analysis or equivalence test is reported, so 'the difference is gone' and 'we could not detect it' are not separated.

The uncorrected 9 comparisons cut both ways. The authors invoke Type I inflation only as a caveat, but the single positive finding (/ap:a/, R4/R5) is exactly what that inflation threatens; the nulls are not at risk from it.

RQ1 ran on N=91 EEG, RQ2 on N=84 combined M/EEG. The brain-behaviour null is therefore on a different and smaller sample than the group-difference finding, which slightly weakens reading them as one developmental story.

The Matthew-effect contrast (I2) rests on a non-significant interaction with N=82 spread over three groups, one of which has 17 members. Low power makes 'no widening' the expected outcome regardless of the truth.

R4 and R7 are compared against Lohvansuu et al. (2014) rather than re-analysed jointly, even though 79 participants have EEG at both ages. A within-subject age x feature test appears possible with the data described and is not reported.

figure_pointers.use: R2 -- reading fluency and accuracy, childhood to adulthood, three group lines. Look at whether the three lines stay parallel: that parallelism is the whole Matthew-effect argument.
M1, R1 -- group sizes and behavioural means. Read the footnote symbols; they carry the pairwise comparisons.
M2 -- the oddball design. Needed before any result makes sense.
M3 -- where in the pseudoword the deviant feature sits. Compare the silent gap between /ata/ and /at:a/.
R3 -- grand-average waveform and topographies, all participants pooled. Panel A for component latencies, panel B for scalp distribution.
R4, R5 -- THE result figure. Masked colour boxes mark significant clusters; yellow stars in C and D mark the channels. Check that the effect is only in the /ap:a/ row.
R4-R7 -- waveforms at Fz split by group. Compare the green (/ap:a/) curve across panels A, B, C.
R7 -- same data regrouped by speech sound. Panel B (/ata/) is where the childhood effect used to be and is now flat.
R8 -- source localisation. Confirms auditory-cortex origin.
R9 -- the 12 correlation histograms with the +-0.215 threshold marked. This figure is what turns a null into a positive demonstration of absence.
